title: History · Non-exam content (Terms 1–3)
exam_focus: Content outside the Yearly exam: Holocaust source-analysis skills, Cold War containment policy (Truman, Eisenhower, Kennedy), and the US and Australian civil rights movements. For revising Term 1–3 concepts and practising source skills.

questions.stem: The Holocaust practice questions set out three steps for 'accounting for the perspective' of a source. After stating what the perspective is, what must you do next?
options: Explain how the perspective appears in the source and why it is there
Describe how long the source is, where it was published and who wrote it
State whether the source is a primary or secondary source
Summarise the source in one sentence without using its evidence
questions.explanation_en: The material sets out three steps: first, identify the perspective; then explain how that perspective is presented in the source and why; simply summarising content without analysing perspective is a common way to lose marks.
questions.source: Term 1 · Practice Questions.pdf — Account for the perspective of Source A

questions.stem: In the Lessons 3.2–4.1 sequence, the Einsatzgruppen are described as which of the following?
options: Mobile killing squads
The Gestapo secret police
Camp-based killing units
Jewish resistance fighters
questions.explanation_en: The lesson is titled 'The Einsatzgruppen — mobile killing squads'. They followed the German army into Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union and killed on a large scale through mass shootings, a different form of killing from the concentration camp system.

questions.stem: A 1934 Nazi propaganda image shows a Jewish man as greedy and physically repellent while a German family looks healthy and prosperous. Which conclusion is most defensible for a historian?
options: It shows the regime's dehumanising portrayal, not how Jews lived
It proves German families were wealthier than Jewish families in 1934
It is too one-sided to be of much use to any historian
It shows that antisemitism only began in Germany in 1934
questions.explanation_en: The value of a propaganda poster lies in what it reveals about the intentions of its creators and the stereotypes they promoted, not in the facts it states. Choosing 'no value' is the typical mistake: bias is itself important evidence about Nazi ideology.
questions.source: Term 1 · Lesson 1.3 Nazi propaganda & the skill of perspective

questions.stem: Explain why a historian studying Kristallnacht might still find a source produced by a Nazi official valuable, even though it is biased.
questions.answer: It reveals the perpetrator's perspective, language and motives — what the regime wanted its audience to believe and how it justified the attacks. The bias is itself evidence of Nazi intent, but the source must be checked against other evidence, such as victim testimony.
questions.explanation_en: Bias does not mean a source has no value: the perpetrator's perspective can reveal propaganda intentions and motives, but it must be used alongside other evidence such as victim testimony. Answers should attend to 'who and why', not simply to true or false.
questions.source: Term 1 · Practice Questions.pdf / Lesson 4.1 Propaganda value source analysis

criteria.t: Explains that the source reveals the perpetrator's perspective, language and motives — what the regime wanted its audience to believe and how it justified the attacks
Argues that the bias is itself evidence of Nazi intent and values
States that the source must be checked against other evidence, such as victim testimony

questions.stem: Distinguish between a source's content and its perspective, and explain why a historian needs both.
questions.answer: Content is what the source says or shows — the events, people and details in it. Perspective is the point of view from which it was made, shaped by the author's side, purpose and audience. A historian needs the content as evidence and the perspective to judge how far that evidence can be trusted.
questions.explanation_en: Content answers 'what was said'; perspective answers 'who said it, from which side, and why'. Keeping the two apart lets you both use the source and evaluate it.
questions.source: Term 1 · Source Analysis Study Notes / Practice Questions

criteria.t: Defines content as what the source says or shows — the events, people and details in it
Defines perspective as the point of view from which the source was made, shaped by the author's side, purpose and audience
Explains that a historian needs the content as evidence and the perspective to judge how far that evidence can be trusted

questions.stem: Which conference does Lesson 2.1 use as the starting point for explaining how the Cold War began?
options: The Potsdam Conference
The Yalta Conference
The Versailles Conference
The Geneva Conference
questions.explanation_en: The lesson sets out to understand the Potsdam Conference and its role in creating the Cold War conflict. The Yalta Conference also took place near the end of the war, but the course starts with Potsdam.
questions.source: Term 2 · Lesson 2.1 Origins of the Cold War (Potsdam Conference)

questions.topic: Cold War · Marshall Plan and NATO
questions.stem: Which pairing correctly matches the two containment instruments taught in Lesson 2.3?
options: Marshall Plan — economic aid; NATO — collective security alliance
Marshall Plan — military alliance; NATO — economic aid program
Marshall Plan — covert CIA action; NATO — nuclear sharing
Marshall Plan — cultural exchange; NATO — trade agreement
questions.explanation_en: The Marshall Plan used economic aid to rebuild Western Europe and reduce the appeal of communism, while NATO (1949) was a collective security alliance. Together they formed the containment system in Europe.
questions.source: Term 2 · Lesson 2.3 The Policy of Containment in Europe — Marshall Plan & NATO

questions.stem: What was the immediate result of the Berlin Crisis of 1961?
options: The building of the Berlin Wall, dividing East from West Berlin
The reunification of Germany under a single government
The withdrawal of all Soviet troops from East Germany
The signing of a formal peace treaty ending the Cold War
questions.explanation_en: In the 1961 Berlin Crisis, East Germany built the Berlin Wall with Soviet support to stop the outflow of its population, and the wall became a symbol of the Cold War division of Europe.

questions.stem: Explain one significant difference between Truman's and Eisenhower's methods of containing communism.
questions.answer: Truman relied mainly on economic and military aid (the Truman Doctrine, the Marshall Plan) and on collective security through NATO, plus a limited conventional war in Korea. Eisenhower preferred nuclear deterrence, brinkmanship and covert CIA action because it contained communism at a lower cost.
questions.explanation_en: The difference lies in means and cost: Truman relied on economic aid and alliances, while Eisenhower relied on nuclear deterrence and covert operations. Answers also need the specific policy names.

criteria.t: Identifies Truman's method as mainly economic and military aid (Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan) and collective security through NATO, plus a limited conventional war in Korea
Identifies Eisenhower's method as nuclear deterrence, brinkmanship and covert CIA action
Explains the significance of the difference: Eisenhower's approach contained communism at a lower cost

questions.stem: Explain why the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 is treated as the most dangerous moment of the Cold War.
questions.answer: The discovery of Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba led to a US naval quarantine and a direct superpower standoff in which any miscalculation could have triggered nuclear war. It ended with the Soviet withdrawal of the missiles and a US pledge not to invade Cuba, and it pushed both sides towards arms control.
questions.explanation_en: The danger was direct confrontation between two nuclear powers with very little decision time. The outcome was the Soviet withdrawal of the missiles, a US promise not to invade Cuba (and a secret US withdrawal of missiles from Turkey), and a move towards arms-control talks.
questions.source: Term 2 · Lesson 5.3 JFK and the Cuban Missile Crisis (1962)

criteria.t: Explains that the discovery of Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba led to a US naval quarantine and a direct superpower standoff
Explains why it was so dangerous: two nuclear-armed superpowers faced each other directly and any miscalculation could have triggered nuclear war
Describes the resolution and its aftermath: Soviet withdrawal of the missiles, a US pledge not to invade Cuba, and a push towards arms control

questions.topic: Civil rights · Universal Declaration of Human Rights
questions.stem: Lesson 1.2 examines the significance of the UDHR. Which description of the UDHR is correct?
options: A 1948 UN declaration of fundamental rights that influenced later conventions
A treaty signed only by the United States and the Soviet Union in 1948
A document listing the punishments given at the Nuremberg Trials
An Australian law passed in 1948 that ended the White Australia Policy
questions.explanation_en: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1948, is not a treaty. It provides the normative basis for later human rights conventions and for domestic law, and that is where its significance lies.
questions.source: Term 3 · Lesson 1.2 The significance of the UDHR to human rights & freedoms

questions.stem: According to the Significant Individuals list in the assessment guide, who led the 1965 Freedom Ride?
options: Charles Perkins
Vincent Lingiari
Eddie Koiki Mabo
William Cooper
questions.explanation_en: The material states clearly that Charles Perkins led the 1965 Freedom Ride. The other figures pair with the 1966 Wave Hill strike (Lingiari), the 1992 Mabo case and the 1938 Day of Mourning (Cooper).
questions.source: Term 3 · Civil Rights Comic Book Assessment Guide — Significant Individuals

questions.topic: Civil rights · Mabo and native title
questions.stem: Which statement explains the significance of Eddie Koiki Mabo's case (1992)?
options: It overturned terra nullius and recognised native title in law
It gave Aboriginal Australians the right to vote in elections
It ended the forced removal of Aboriginal children from families
It created the first Aboriginal community-controlled health service
questions.explanation_en: The Mabo decision rejected the legal doctrine of 'terra nullius' and recognised the land rights of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, which was a turning point in the land rights movement.
questions.source: Term 3 · Assessment Guide — Significant Individuals (Eddie Koiki Mabo)

questions.stem: Explain what is meant by the 'Stolen Generations'.
questions.answer: They are the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children who were forcibly removed from their families by government agencies and church missions under protection and welfare laws, mainly across the twentieth century. The removals broke families and caused long-term trauma that still affects communities.
questions.explanation_en: The key point is forced removal rather than voluntary departure, carried out under state protection and welfare laws, with family disruption and intergenerational trauma as the result.

criteria.t: Identifies the Stolen Generations as Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children who were forcibly removed from their families
Explains that the removals were carried out by government agencies and church missions under protection and welfare laws, mainly across the twentieth century
Explains the consequence: the removals broke families and caused long-term trauma that still affects communities

questions.topic: Civil rights · Land rights and native title
questions.stem: Distinguish between 'land rights' and 'native title' as used in Lesson 5.3.
questions.answer: Land rights are grants or recognition of land by government legislation — land returned or given to Aboriginal communities. Native title is a right recognised by the courts as belonging to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples whose traditional laws and customs connect them to the land; it is understood to have survived colonisation rather than being granted.
questions.explanation_en: The crucial difference lies in the source: land rights come from legislation and government grants, while native title comes from court-recognised traditional rights existing before colonisation (the Mabo decision).
questions.source: Term 3 · Lesson 5.3 The Significance of the Land Rights Movement & Native Title

criteria.t: Explains that land rights are grants or recognition of land by government legislation — land returned or given to Aboriginal communities
Explains that native title is a right recognised by the courts, belonging to peoples whose traditional laws and customs connect them to the land
Distinguishes the source of each right: native title is understood to have survived colonisation rather than being granted
